title: Building VitalCore Hospital in Unity with Claude Code: real gameplay, screenshots, and the hard part of AI-assisted simulation
author: Consistent_Banana_59
selftext:
I'm a solo developer working on VitalCore Hospital in Unity, with Claude Code and AI assistance helping me build and debug it. I wanted to share the actual game and talk about the part of this process that has been hardest: getting a lot of interacting simulation systems to stay consistent.



The idea is a hospital builder where you can also go down to the floor in first person and take part in patient care. The overhead side covers rooms, departments, staffing and hospital operations. The challenge is making those management decisions connect to what happens to an individual patient, rather than having two unrelated games sharing a building.



When I started, the first ten hours were scripting and basic shapes. AI assistance hasn't made the project appear in one prompt. It has helped with implementing systems, investigating bugs and reviewing how pieces fit together, but the work still comes back to opening Unity, running the hospital and finding out what actually happens.



A concrete example is the patient lifecycle. A patient isn't just a character walking to a waypoint: they can hold a seat reservation, a bed, a room slot and a queued job. Discharge, a failed check-in, a transfer timeout or rebuilding a room can leave stale ownership behind if those systems don't agree on when care has ended. Recent development work has focused on shared checks and coordinated cleanup, along with restoring treatment progress and bed placement after loading. That's a much less glamorous problem than adding another department, but it matters to whether a hospital keeps working after a long session.



The management screens expose another integration challenge. A staff member being employed doesn't mean their department is covered at the right time. Scheduling, handoffs, recruitment and retention have to connect back to care. The clinical-risk side adds another layer: the player needs to understand how an incident relates to what happened on the floor, rather than feeling like a random penalty appeared in an office menu.



My biggest lesson so far is that generating a plausible implementation and verifying a simulation are different jobs. A system can look fine in isolation while a save/load, interrupted task or room rebuild breaks the assumptions between systems. I'm still working on reliability and longer sessions; this is an alpha, not a claim that every lifecycle or save issue is solved.



The video and screenshots below are real gameplay from the October 29 development capture, not generated gameplay footage or concept art. The tour uses AI narration. Development footage can include changes beyond the live Steam Playtest.



I'd be interested in how other people here validate AI-assisted simulation projects. What has helped you catch problems that only show up when several systems interact, or when a save is reloaded halfway through a task?



For anyone who wants to follow the project, the Steam page is https://store.steampowered.com/app/5342330/ and the full tour is also on YouTube: https://youtu.be/3EY73HvBbN8

comments.author: office-canard
comments.body:
My games are much smaller than yours, so take this with a grain of salt. Claude started writing headless test harnesses in Node.js on its own, without me asking, and now nothing ships until a build passes them. They check the logic, things like whether every level is actually solvable and whether the physics behaves.



But a harness only checks what you thought to check. The problems that slip through are the ones I find by playing. So I split the job: the machine checks the logic, and I check the feel. I agree with your lesson. Making something that looks right and proving it is right are different jobs.
